blocks.text: Consider an AC circuit containing a resistor R and inductor L connected in series with an AC source V as shown in Fig.17.10(a). As R and L are in series, therefore, same current I flows through both R and L.
Let rms value of current through R is I. Then rms value of voltage V_R across R will be:
V will be in phase with the current I in the circuit, as R is shown vectorially by line OA in Fig.17.10(c). The value of rms voltage V_L across L will be:

Voltage V across L is ahead of current I through L by 90° as shown in Fig.17.10 (b) and vectorially by line OB in Fig.17.10(c). The resultant voltage V will be the vector sum of V_R and V_L shown vectorially by line OP, thus in Fig.17.10(c):

blocks.alt: (a) A resistor R and inductor L in series with an AC supply V (+ and -); current I flows round the circuit; double arrows mark VR across R and VL across L. (b) Voltage V and current I against omega t from 0 to 360 degrees, with the same period; V leads I by theta. (c) Vector diagram OABP: OA = VR along the current I (R), OB = AP = VL (XL = wL) at right angles, and the diagonal OP = V = IZ at angle theta.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 17.10(b) draws voltage and current 90° apart and at different frequencies, and (c) labels OA 'V'. Both have the same frequency, the voltage leads by θ (tan θ = ωL/R), and OA is V_R, as drawn above.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The squares belong outside the brackets: Vᵣₘₛ = √((IᵣₘₛR)² + (IᵣₘₛX_L)²) = Iᵣₘₛ√(R² + X_L²), as the next line uses.

blocks.text_alt: As X_L = ωL, so Vᵣₘₛ = Iᵣₘₛ √(R² + (ωL)²)

blocks.text: The angle θ which Z makes with R line, gives the phase difference between the applied voltage and current.

blocks.text: The specialised cells of the electric eel are called electrocytes, not electrolytes (an electrolyte is a solution that conducts electricity).
